chapter_theme: The second half of the neythal section: the friend refuses the shore lord's night visits because the pearls light the village, the tide rises and both day and night carry danger (48, 49, 55, 59), turns the shore into a marshalled royal army to press for a fixed wedding day (50, 52-54), points out the grove and the house where they may meet (56, 58, 61), while the hero names the fisher girl who has maddened him (60), the heroine refuses him (57) and the friend praises the man who once helped them (62).

48.reading: Where the waves have come up and drawn back from the clear backwater grove, the fragrant fishing village has for its lamp the pearls that open-mouthed, green-backed oysters cast on the shore, which drive off the dark as the sun goes down.
48.nuance: The verse names no speaker or hearer; read beside 49, which turns the same pearl-light into a question to the shore lord, the lit village is a reason he cannot come unseen by night. The praise of the shore's riches is also a warning.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and the fishing village at nightfall

comparisons.tenor: the pearls on the shore, which serve the village as its lamp

49.reading: The friend asks the lord of the cool, broad backwater where he thinks he will come, into a village where pearls breathed out by conches that the surging waves have kicked ashore sweep away even the midnight dark.
49.nuance: The objection to the night visit is not the usual dark and its beasts but light: the shore is so rich that its pearls undo the midnight that should hide him. எங்கு வருதி is a refusal shaped as a question.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the shore lord and the fishing village

50.reading: With boats for elephants, waves for drums and the many birds that rise and break the sleep of the shore for an army, the lord of the lovely sea is asked to give up coming without a set tryst, like sleep, and to take her by the proper way.
50.nuance: The two images pull against each other: the shore is arrayed like a royal army that marches in order, while he comes like sleep, by stealth and without a tryst. The friend asks him to match the order of his own shore (நெறியால் நீ கொள்வது).

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the fishing boats

comparisons.vehicle: திமில்களி றாகத் திரைபறையாப் பல்புள் துயில்கெடத் தோன்றும் படையா
comparisons.tenor: the shore at daybreak, its boats, waves and birds marshalled like a king's elephants, drums and troops
his coming unannounced, unbidden as sleep

51.reading: On the white sand of the grove that reeks of fish, we watch the catch and sell it, and over all the adumbu creepers nets like coats of mail lie drying while the flowers bloom thick about them.
51.nuance: The speaker counts herself among the fish-sellers (பகர்தும், we sell): naming the smell and the trade is how the neythal friend reminds a well-born suitor of the distance between them, though the same chore can also mark the place where she may be met by day.

thinai_evidence.note: fish, nets and adumbu creeper of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the fishing nets spread on the creepers, meshed like chain mail

52.reading: Lord of the sea shore, where with the waves for mahouts, the boats for elephants and the grove on the bank for troops the scene stands like a king roused but unhurried: to choose a day and marry her is right.
52.nuance: விரையாது carries the argument: a king does not rush to war but rises in order, and so the lord of such a shore should not rush to the grove at night but fix a day (நாள் ஆய்ந்து). Marriage is called அறம், a duty and not only a kindness.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the shore grove

comparisons.vehicle: திரைபாக னாகத் திமில்களி றாகக் கரைசேர்ந்த கானல் படையா
comparisons.tenor: the shore's waves, boats and grove marshalled as a king's force
the whole shore, risen in order like a king who musters without haste

53.reading: Lord of the sea shore, where with ships for horses, long boats for many elephants, clear waves for drums and birds for troops the scene is like a restless king risen to war: make sure you come forward before our kin rise first.
53.nuance: எமர் முன்கிளர்ந்து may mean that he should rise before our kin do (to give her elsewhere, or against him), or that he should come forward before our kin to ask for her; either way the restless king of the image is a pressure, not the calm one of 52.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea lord and the long fishing boats

comparisons.vehicle: பாறு புரவியாப் பல்களிறு நீள்திமிலாத்தேறு திரைபறையாப் புட்படையாத்
comparisons.tenor: the shore's ships, boats, waves and birds marshalled as a king's horse, elephants, drums and troops
the whole shore, astir like a king who has risen and will not settle

54.reading: You come, but on the fine sand of the backwater grove the legs of your chariot horses sink, which is a harm; on reflection you need seek no other plan: call those who read omens, choose a day and give yourself to her, which is good.
54.nuance: The friend turns a fact of the shore (horses sink in the sand) into a reason for a public road to her: the secret way is literally unsound under his chariot, and the sound way is the diviners' fixed day. கொண்டோர் is hard to place; it may name the kin who take the bride.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater grove and its fine sand

55.reading: Look about you: the cold dew is harsh, and the great dark spreads over the land; do not come in your swift chariot when the water floods the ways, for if you come she will not bear it, facing the rising tide.
55.nuance: The danger is put in her, not in him: வரின் ஆற்றாள், if you come she will not endure it. The friend forbids the night visit by making the heroine's fear for him the cost of his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the rising tide on the shore at night

56.reading: Lord of the sea grove, where the punnai of the grove that stretches along the backwater bends low and shades, and the anril calls from the lovely tall palmyras of the frond-thick grove crowding the young sand of our front yard.
56.nuance: The friend gives the shore lord the marks of their house (எம் முன்றில்): the drooping punnai and the palmyras where the anril calls. The anril, the bird that cannot bear parting from its mate, is the traditional sign of her nights; it only calls here and does nothing a lover does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, anril and palmyra of the shore

57.reading: Lord of the roaring sea, whose long-sanded grove the coming waves roam and whose plenty no single wave runs off from, where two waves at once fall before the grove: you need not desire me any more.
57.nuance: The waves that come and fall, two at a time, may hint at a man whose comings are divided; the poem does not say so, and the image gives only one match of mood, so it is not tagged as ullurai. The last line is a refusal in the heroine's own voice (என்), not the friend's.

thinai_evidence.note: the long sand of the grove and the sea lord

58.reading: Do you not see the rolling sea and the white sand that lies against the grove, together like Mayavan and his elder brother, and the grove filled through its middle with njazhal and screw-pine and all round with punnai, flowering gladly?
58.nuance: The dark god and his white elder brother give the shore its two colours, dark sea and white sand, joined as brothers are. Mayavan is the god of the mullai land, so the simile brings a mullai deity onto the neythal shore. காணாயோ invites the hearer into the grove, which reads as pointing out a meeting place.

thinai_evidence.note: njazhal, screw-pine and punnai of the shore grove

comparisons.tenor: the dark sea and the white sand lying side by side

59.reading: If you come by day the gossip will be great, and if you come by night without care the dangers are as great; the home of the poor fisherfolk is on the wave-beaten shore where the screw-pine, hard to pass through, sways.
59.nuance: Both trysts are refused at once, day for the gossip and night for the danger, which leaves only marriage open, though the friend never names it. ஏழை நுளையர், the poor fisherfolk, adds the modesty of class to the refusal.

thinai_evidence.note: the screw-pine shore and the fisher folk

60.reading: Where the waves cry out and will not leave but shout and wander, and the shore crab marks the sand with its legs, the long-eyed girl plucking neythal flowers near the shore is the fisherman's daughter who has made me mad with love.
60.nuance: The waves that cry, will not go and wander are the hero's own state set out before he names its cause; the closing word மையல் (madness of love) is placed on the girl, not on himself. She is identified by her people, நுளையர் மகள், which is all the lover knows of her.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal flower, crab and fisher folk

61.reading: Lord of the sounding sea, it is hard for anyone to know of it, for no one strays along that path: there is nothing there but the backwater ringed by kandal with turning shoots and cool thillai mingled, and the dense cool screw-pine joined among them.
61.nuance: Read as the friend naming a meeting place, the thicket of kandal, thillai and screw-pine is safe because no one walks there; the same words could be a warning that the way is pathless. இல்லை in line 2 has no stated subject.

thinai_evidence.note: kandal, thillai and screw-pine of the backwater

62.reading: Neither at the bowmen's festivals nor at the festivals of fine people in this sea-girt world have we seen his like; good girl, if there are any in heaven to match the shore lord who once helped us in the salt land, consider it.
62.nuance: The help (உதவி) is the founding act of the love, the once-only service in the salt pans; the praise ranks him above earth and sets heaven as the only place left to search, which makes a debt of gratitude into the measure of a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the salt land and the shore lord

links.note: 48 describes the pearl-lit village at nightfall with no hearer; 49 addresses the shore lord with the same pearls dispelling the midnight dark and asks where he will come.
links.teaches: Read together, the bare description of 48 gains its speech act from 49: the pearl-light that seems praise of the shore's riches is the friend's ground for refusing the night tryst.

links.note: Akananuru 80: the friend says he has come by night across the dark backwater of crocodiles and sharks and asks him to come by day to the grove where they guard drying fish. Thinaimalai 49: no dark at all to cross, since the pearls sweep away the midnight.
links.teaches: The two friends refuse the same night visit for opposite reasons, the older one because the dark hides beasts and the venba because the shore has no dark to hide him, so the convention needs only the refusal and lets the reason be turned inside out.

links.note: 50 sets the hero's stealthy coming, like sleep and without a tryst, against the proper way; 52, with the same shore-army image, names the proper way: choose a day and marry.
links.teaches: The vague நெறியால் of 50 is spelled out in 52 as நாள் ஆய்ந்து வரைதல், so the sequence moves from forbidding the secret visit to prescribing the rite, with the marshalled shore as the model of order in both.

links.note: 52: the shore is like a king who rises without haste, so fix a day. 53: the shore is like a king who has risen and will not settle, so come before our kin move.
links.teaches: One image of the shore as a royal army is given opposite tempos, unhurried and restless, to argue first for deliberation and then for urgency, which shows the poet using the image to set the pace of the plea rather than to carry a fixed sense.

links.note: Purananuru 42: the Chola's army roars like the sea. Thinaimalai 52: the sea, with waves for mahouts and boats for elephants, is like a king's force rising.
links.teaches: The puram simile is run backwards in the neythal venba: where the war poem makes an army sound like the sea, the love poem makes the sea a mustered army, so that the shore lord is held to a king's measured conduct and the wedding becomes his orderly campaign.

links.note: Natrinai 45: the friend tells the rich man's son that they are fishermen's daughters who drive birds from drying shark and smell of fish (புலவு நாறுதும்), so their life is no match for his. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish on the sand that reeks of it.
links.teaches: The venba keeps only the smell and the trade and drops the explicit 'go away, we are not your equals' of the Natrinai, which shows how far the later poet could rely on the reader supplying the refusal from the fish-smell alone.

links.note: Akananuru 80: the friend tells the shore lord that they guard their father's drying fish from birds in the punnai grove and asks him to come there by day. Thinaimalai 51: we watch and sell the fish in the grove.
links.teaches: The same chore that in Natrinai 45 marks the girls as beneath the suitor is in Akananuru 80 the cover for a daytime meeting, so the venba's bare picture of fish-watching could be either a rebuff or an invitation, which is why its sense stays open.

links.note: Akananuru 86: the husband recalls the wedding held at a bright dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet on a faultless day. Thinaimalai 54: the friend tells the hero to call the diviners and choose a day.
links.teaches: The diviners' day that the friend demands in the venba is the day the older poem remembers by the moon's freedom from the planet, so the pair shows the omen-reading as the hinge that turns the secret tryst into the public rite.

links.note: Natrinai 303: the heroine lies sleepless at each cry of the anril joined with its mate in the palmyra of the common ground. Thinaimalai 56: the friend tells the shore lord that the anril calls from the tall palmyras of their front yard.
links.teaches: Natrinai 303 shows what the anril's cry does to the heroine at midnight, so when the friend in the venba points the hero to the anril in their own yard she is telling him, without saying so, what the girl hears each night he is away.

links.note: Kalittokai 124: the white waves ring the white dune like the blue garment worn by the milk-white elder brother of the god who measured the world. Thinaimalai 58: the dark sea and the white sand lie together like Mayavan and his elder brother.
links.teaches: Both neythal poets read the shore's dark and white through the two divine brothers, but Kalittokai puts both colours on the one white brother in his blue cloth, while the venba splits them between the two brothers, so the sea and the sand become kin rather than body and garment.

links.note: Kuruntokai 217: the friend tells the hill lord that meeting by day is possible while they guard the millet, but she fears his coming by night. Thinaimalai 59: by day the gossip is great, and by night the dangers are as great.
links.teaches: The Kuruntokai friend still leaves the day open and fears only the night, while the venba's friend closes both, so the pair shows the second step of the convention, where barring day and night together leaves marriage as the only way.

links.note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும்). Thinaimalai 60: the hero names the long-eyed girl plucking neythal as the fisherman's daughter who has made him mad (மையல்).
links.teaches: The couplet's lover reels because he cannot tell what she is, while the venba's lover knows exactly who she is, a fisherman's daughter at the shore, and is mad all the same, so the scene shows the bewilderment surviving the answer to the Kural's question.

links.note: Kural 101: for help given unasked, earth and heaven together are hardly a return. Thinaimalai 62: no one on this sea-girt earth matches the shore lord who once helped in the salt land; seek his equal in heaven.
links.teaches: The venba takes the Kural's measure of unrequited help, earth and heaven, and applies it to the helper himself: the lover's one service makes him without equal in either world, so the ethical rule of gratitude becomes the friend's argument for the man.

source_issues: 48-62: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems, and occasion.words is null throughout.
49 line 3: நரன்யியிர்த்த is corrupt; நரல் உயிர்த்த (breathed out by the sounding conch) fits the sense. Line 4 வரன்றுயிர்த்த is unclear.
51 line 4: பாலிகை is unclear here (a pot of sprouted seed is its usual sense); read as a flower of the shore.
53 line 1: நீள்திமிலாத்தேறு joins நீள்திமிலா(த்) and தேறு, which begins the next phrase (தேறு திரைபறையா); a spacing error.
56 line 2: அடற்கானல் is odd; அடர் கானல் (dense grove) may be meant.
60 line 2: காலினாற் கானாக் is unclear; a verb for the crab marking or scratching the sand with its legs is expected.
62 line 3: ஒரோஉதவி may be ஒரோஉ உதவி (a single help) or ஓர் உதவி; the sense, one past act of help, holds either way.
